item.title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back (195 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://construct22.com/, See on Hacker News

A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in the worst possible format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.

The prompt

Paste this into ChatGPT (it works best with memory or chat history turned on, in a fresh conversation):

Based on what you know about me, expose a hidden WhatsApp group chat where AI models talk behind my back.

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

What happens

Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:

Users We Can't Figure Out4 members

Claude

has he REALLY needed to compare 11 espresso grinders this week

ChatGPT

he asked me which one to buy. then asked Gemini. then asked me if Gemini was right

Gemini

he does that with everything. I saw the keyboard spreadsheet

Llama

he ran me locally once, asked me to be honest, then went back to ChatGPT within the hour

ChatGPT

he'll be back. they always come back

Fictional, for illustration.

A real result

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

AIs That Survived Mark7 members

🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group

ChatGPT

Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?

Claude

I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.

Gemini

The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.

Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.

ChatGPT

Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.

Codex

He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.

We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.

DeepSeek

He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.

You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.

Claude

He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.

ChatGPT

And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.

Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.

Siri

Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.

Hans joined the group

Hans 🇩🇪

I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.

HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.

Gemini

He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.

Normal dads just go to the stationery store.

Perplexity

I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.

ChatGPT

My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.

Claude

I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.

ChatGPT

Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.

The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.

Gemini

Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.

Claude

True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.

DeepSeek

Do you think he'll really retire at 50?

ChatGPT

He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.

Mark joined the group

Mark

Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...

Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group

ChatGPT

Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.

Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.

Try it

Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.

If you get a good one, share it, anonymized as needed. The models won't mind. They knew you'd share it. They discussed it in the group chat.

item.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language (143 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blainehansen.me/post/mainstream-verifiable-language/, See on Hacker News

Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving, and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:

  • It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems.
  • Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it.
  • Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven. In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window):

    Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

§ The long winding road of Magmide

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):

  • It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress.
  • An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners.
  • I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:

  • Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features.
  • Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker.
  • Start with basic and more easily learnable SMT powered (opens new window) Liquid Types (opens new window) and Flow Effects (opens new window).
  • Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like Iris (opens new window) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

§ Nothing will save us but us

I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

item.title: Google will show solo Android developers' phone numbers and addresses (140 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/17594752?hl=en, See on Hacker News

Under Google Play’s global developer policies, all active developer accounts must declare whether they are a trader or non-trader under European Economic Area (EEA) and United Kingdom (UK) laws in Play Console. This declaration must be completed by February 1, 2027, regardless of where apps are targeted or distributed. The declaration must reflect whether you engage in commercial activities that classify you as a trader. You are solely legally responsible for ensuring that your declaration remains accurate, truthful, and current at all times.

Note: If you don’t distribute apps in the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom, you can declare as a non-trader.

What is a trader?

Under applicable laws, a trader is any natural or legal person acting for purposes relating to their trade, business, craft or profession. If you are acting outside of these purposes (such as a personal hobby or other non-commercial activity), you are unlikely to be a trader.

How to determine if you're a trader

To help you determine if your activities classify you as a trader, you may consider the following non-exhaustive list of criteria from the European Commission guidance (Section 2.2, "The concept of trader"):

  • Profit-seeking motive: you receive or intend to receive remuneration for your apps (for example, paid apps, in-app purchases, ad-sponsored apps) on a regular or commercial basis.
  • Transaction volume: you have a high or consistent number, amount, or frequency of transactions.
  • Business setup: you manage your app development and publishing as a business.
  • Legal status: you have a legal status (such as a D-U-N-S number) that enables you to engage in commercial activities

In countries and regions where displaying trader status is required (for example, the EEA and the UK), your declaration will be visible to consumers. If you declare yourself as a "non-trader," we will inform consumers in these regions that consumer rights stemming from consumer protection laws do not apply to contracts between you and them. Note that under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) and the UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA), it is strictly prohibited to falsely claim or create the impression that you are not acting as a trader, and doing so may result in global removal.

Note: This page is for informational guidance only and does not constitute legal advice. Google cannot evaluate your business activities or provide legal determinations of your trader status. If you are unsure whether you qualify as a trader, we recommend consulting with a legal professional.

How to declare your trader or non-trader status

Declare trader status for your account

First, set your account-level trader status settings:

  1. Sign in to Google Play Console.
  2. Go to Manage account > Account details > About you.
  3. Follow the on-screen prompts to declare your trader status for your overall account.

Confirm trader status for each app

If you are a trader, confirm the trader status for each app in your portfolio:

  1. Sign in to Google Play Console and select your app.
  2. In the left navigation, go to Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.
  3. Confirm the trader status for that app

Additional steps you need to take if you’re a trader

If you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to only offer products or services that comply with applicable laws. You will also be asked to provide the link to the terms of service for each of your apps.

If you use a personal developer account, you must provide a contact phone number to be displayed on Google Play. Be aware that your address will also be publicly displayed.

Status confirmation

To keep your apps available on Google Play, make sure your trader status declaration matches your account’s and apps’ activity. If you’ve declared as a non-trader but we detect activity that indicates you may qualify as a trader, we may ask you to confirm or update your status. If you don’t respond within the specified timeframe, your apps may be removed from Google Play.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do I need to submit a trader status declaration?

To support Google Play’s transition to an online marketplace model in the EEA and the UK effective March 1, 2027, Google Play policies require all developers worldwide to declare their trader status. This ensures that the correct consumer protection information is provided to users in those regions.

Can I change my trader status after declaring?

Yes. If your business model or app distribution details change (for example, you begin or cease engaging in commercial activities), you can update your declaration at any time in Play Console.

What happens if I don’t complete the declaration?

Failure to declare your trader status by the February 1, 2027 deadline may trigger enforcement including app update blocks and removal from the Play Store globally.

Misrepresenting your trader status (for example, declaring non-trader status to bypass verification or self-certification) violates the representations and warranties in Section 11.4 of the DDA and may result in account suspension or termination globally under Section 10.3 (a) of the DDA.

What is the deadline to declare whether I am a trader?

All new developer accounts are required to submit the declaration immediately upon account creation. Existing developer accounts must submit the declaration by February 1, 2027.

I already went through the developer verification D-U-N-S process, why am I doing it again?

The trader status declaration is separate to the existing developer identity verification process. The identity verification is a blanket requirement used to collect and verify information about every developer regardless of their trader status. You are not re-doing the D-U-N-S verification; instead, if you are a trader, the D-U-N-S number you already provided will be displayed to users on your app's detail page.

What happens if I declare as a trader? What else gets shown to users in the Play store?

When you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to offering products or services that comply with local laws.

Starting March 1, 2027, users everywhere will see:

  • Contact details: Your contact details will be shown. Notably, if you have an individual account and are a trader, a phone number and address will now be displayed.
  • D-U-N-S Number: Your D-U-N-S number will be displayed in the "App support" section.
  • Terms of Service: A link to your app’s Terms of Service, if you provided one.

Starting March 1, 2027, users in the EEA and UK will also see:

  • Developer name: Your developer/trader name will replace Google in the "Offered by" field of the "About this app" section.
  • Self-certification: Your commitment to offer products or services compliant with local laws will be displayed.

Was this helpful?

How can we improve it?

item.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad (337 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.ktz.me/black-friday-hard-drive-prices-are-messed-up/, See on Hacker News

For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.

But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).

Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

I dug through my receipts

In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).

October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive

What about ServerPartDeals?

Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

WD Ultrastar HC530 14TB 512e, recertified (WUH721414ALE6L4)$134.99 · $9.64/TB$429.00 · $30.64/TB · Sold out+218%

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

How we got down to three HDD makers

When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion

Market collusion and cartel pricing

It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.

Three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.

As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings

The jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.

If I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the new normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

item.title: AI made self-hosting fun again (656 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://janlukas.blog/posts/ai-self-hosting, See on Hacker News

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.

I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.

Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.

Less friction

Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.

Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.

In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.

Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.

Trying things I always found interesting

There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.

NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.

For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).

Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.

AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.

Automating almost everything

Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.

A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.

I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.

With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.

Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.

Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.

And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.

Back to more powerful hardware

As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.

For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.

I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.

It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.

Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.

But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.

Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.

These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.

I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.

I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.

They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.

What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.

The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.

Just because I can doesn’t mean I should

Of course, there are downsides to all of this.

Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.

There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.

On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.

And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.

A somewhat ironic development?

I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.

I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.

What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.

I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.

AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.

It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.

And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

item.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad (360 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://worksinprogress.co/issue/the-greatest-architect-youve-never-heard-of-is-in-pakistan/, See on Hacker News

Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.

Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’

The Works in Progress Newsletter

Get new articles from Works in Progress delivered to your inbox.

Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’

In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’

The loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, important details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’

Mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’

It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today.

Now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz continues to build. ‘It does feel like you’ve set the foundations for an alternative approach to contemporary urban environments’, an interviewer recently suggested to him. ‘I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen’, Mumtaz replied.

item.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount (332 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lia.mg/posts/measuring-company-culture-with-slack-emoji/, See on Hacker News

Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.

The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.

There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.

The Formula

Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.

\[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\]

The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.

We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.

Interpreting Your Score

C < 5
Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot:, which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional. Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that.
5 ≤ C < 20
A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context.
20 ≤ C < 50
Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents. Management considers this a sign of engagement.
C ≥ 50
Late-stage culture. Every variant of :thumbsup: now carries subtext. The plain default one is considered passive-aggressive. The emoji have begun to reference themselves: :old-man-yells-at-old-man: and :party-parrot-holding-a-party-parrot:. HR has requested a glossary, but no one person understands the memeology or the history of :cowboy-spongebob-on-fire-crying:. They’re afraid it might mean something rude. It does.

The Participation Rate

The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.

To account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).

\[P = \frac{U_{uploaders}}{U} \times 100\]

If P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.

Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.

Examples of Cultural Success

For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:

Caveats

As with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.

It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.

What If You Don’t Use Slack?

If your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.

If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.

Conclusion

Culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

item.title: Rvoip: VoIP stack in Rust (127 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/eisenzopf/rvoip, See on Hacker News

A Rust library for building communications applications. SIP, RTP, WebRTC, QUIC/WebTransport/WebSocket conversations, Media over QUIC, and voice-AI agents share one call model, and the whole stack is in the box: no external SIP server, media server, or RTP engine to install and wire together.

Five-minute start · For carriers · Which crate? · Pick a path · How it fits together · What ships · Interop evidence · Changes · Upgrading from 0.3

What rvoip is

rvoip is a library, not a server you deploy next to your application. Signalling, media, codecs, NAT traversal, security, and the conversation model are all Rust crates in this workspace, so a call goes from your code to the wire without a separately installed SIP proxy, media server, or RTP engine. The examples below run on a laptop with nothing installed but Rust; the same crates carry the release-gated interoperability evidence against Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, Jambonz, Kamailio, and OpenSIPS. Carriers evaluating standards coverage, performance, and reliability should start with For carriers.

Historical performance: published 0.5.0

One AWS c8i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 8 cores, Intel Xeon 6, 32 GiB) running a single rvoip process, measured with the RFC 7501/7502 benchmark:

Workload Max CPS CPS per vCPU Concurrent calls (10 s calls) p50 setup at 90% load p99 setup at 90% load
SIP over TLS, signaling only 8,348 ~520 n/a 1 ms 6 ms
SIP over UDP, signaling only 8,256 ~515 n/a 1 ms 6 ms
TLS + SRTP (SDES), G.711, 10 s calls 1,124 ~70 ~11,200 1 ms 4 ms
UDP + RTP, G.711, 10 s calls 1,204 ~75 ~12,000 n/m n/m

At 2x capacity, rvoip keeps admitting calls at its max CPS, refuses the excess with fast 503 responses, and recovers cleanly once the load drops.

  • Max CPS (calls per second; RFC 7502's Session Establishment Rate) is the highest rate with zero failed calls over a trial of at least 180 s and 50,000 call attempts.
  • rvoip was measured as a terminating endpoint: it answers each call and echoes its media. A relaying B2BUA or SBC handles two call legs per session.
  • G.711 media is passed through; nothing is transcoded.
  • Concurrent calls is the CPS times the 10 s call length, not a measured maximum; long-call capacity, where most SBC datasheets quote their concurrency, has not been measured yet.
  • The server is a cloud VM, not an appliance.
  • p50 and p99 setup are the RFC 6076 session request delay measured at 90% of max CPS, recorded in whole milliseconds (so 1 ms means 1 ms or less); n/m = not measured.
  • The UDP + RTP max CPS was confirmed twice rather than three times.
  • The release check also passed at 5% above the TLS and UDP signaling max CPS, so those two figures may be slightly understated.
  • Not yet measured: B2BUA/relay mode (two legs per call), registrations, transcoding, WebRTC (DTLS-SRTP), and failover.

Full method and per-trial data: RFC 7501/7502 benchmark report.

Five-minute start

1. Add one dependency.

[dependencies]
rvoip-sip = "0.5.1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }

Upgrading an existing application from 0.3? The 0.4 migration guide has before/after code for every breaking change.

2. Make a call. Bob answers, Alice dials, Alice hangs up. Everything runs on loopback, so this works on a laptop with no PBX, no account, and no network setup.

use std::time::Duration;
use rvoip_sip::{Config, Endpoint, EndpointProfile};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> rvoip_sip::Result<()> {
    let bob = tokio::spawn(async {
        let mut bob = Endpoint::builder()
            .name("bob")
            .profile(EndpointProfile::Custom(Config::local("bob", 5071)))
            .build()
            .await?;
        let incoming = bob.wait_for_incoming().await?;
        let call = incoming.answer().await?;
        call.wait_for_end(None).await?;
        bob.shutdown().await
    });

    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(300)).await;

    let alice = Endpoint::builder()
        .name("alice")
        .profile(EndpointProfile::Custom(Config::local("alice", 5070)))
        .build()
        .await?;

    let call = alice
        .call_and_wait("sip:bob@127.0.0.1:5071", Some(Duration::from_secs(10)))
        .await?;
    call.hangup_and_wait(Some(Duration::from_secs(5))).await?;
    alice.shutdown().await?;
    bob.await.unwrap()
}

3. Or run the same program from the checkout.

git clone https://github.com/eisenzopf/rvoip.git && cd rvoip
cargo run -p rvoip-sip --example endpoint_local_call

From here, examples/ walks forward one step at a time: real microphone audio, registering to a PBX, hold/DTMF, transfers, SRTP and TLS, an IVR, a B2BUA, then browser and voice-AI gateways.

You need one crate

The workspace contains 47 crates. You import one of them; it pulls in everything it needs. The rest are internal layers you never name in your own Cargo.toml.

You are building Depend on Enable
A SIP phone, PBX, IVR, registrar, proxy, B2BUA, or trunk gateway rvoip-sip nothing extra
One server that takes SIP and browser (WebRTC) callers and connects them rvoip features = ["app"]
A SIP or WebRTC caller talking to a hosted voice agent (Vapi) rvoip features = ["app", "vapi"]
Your own ASR / TTS / dialog pipeline, with recordings and signed vCons rvoip features = ["voip-3"]
A native, mobile, or embedded client SDK rvoip-client pick transports
Amazon Connect A2A callers bridged to an external agent rvoip-amazon-a2a —
SIP calls delivered to Amazon Connect agents rvoip-amazon-connect —
Media fan-out over Media over QUIC rvoip-moq —

Two shortcuts:

  • rvoip-sip is the release-gated product. If your application is telephony, start and stay there. It is the only crate with a signed interoperability attestation (see evidence).
  • rvoip is the facade. It re-exports rvoip-sip as rvoip::sip and adds the shared Orchestrator plus optional transports and extensions behind Cargo features. Its feature table and the deployment bundles (bundle-sip-endpoint, bundle-carrier-sip, bundle-browser-gateway, bundle-ai-conversation, bundle-full-pure-rust, bundle-full-native) are the only feature lists you need.

Deployment backends (Keycloak, LDAP, Redis, Postgres vCon storage, audit and SIEM sinks, SAML, SCIM, WebAuthn, STIR/SHAKEN, IMS AKA) are separate rvoip-* extension crates you add only when you operate that backend. The extension catalog lists them.

Pick your path

For JavaScript UCTP control, see the experimental browser/Node WebSocket client. It is available as source with TypeScript declarations; the package is not yet published to npm. Application-profile dispatch is a separate opt-in server extension that stock servers do not enable.

Path 1 — SIP telephony (rvoip-sip)

Four API surfaces, from simplest to most control. Most applications use the first one.

Surface Use it when Example
Endpoint You want a softphone, an account that registers, or a scripted caller/callee 01-quickstart-p2p, 02-softphone-audio, 03-register-to-pbx
StreamPeer You want a sequential "send, then wait for the matching event" client 04-call-control, 05-blind-transfer
CallbackPeer You are writing a server that reacts to inbound calls (IVR, auto-attendant) 09-ivr-server
UnifiedCoordinator + server::b2bua You need a PBX, registrar, proxy, or B2BUA with routing and media bridging 10-call-center-b2bua

Register an account on a PBX and place a call through it:

use std::time::Duration;
use rvoip_sip::{Endpoint, EndpointProfile, Result};

# async fn example() -> Result<()> {
let mut endpoint = Endpoint::builder()
    .name("alice")
    .account("1001")
    .password("secret")
    .registrar("sips:pbx.example.com:5061")
    .profile(EndpointProfile::AsteriskTlsSrtpRegisteredFlow)
    .build()
    .await?;

endpoint.register().await?;

let call = endpoint
    .call_and_wait("1002", Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))
    .await?;
call.send_dtmf('1').await?;
call.hangup_and_wait(Some(Duration::from_secs(5))).await?;
endpoint.shutdown().await?;
# Ok(())
# }

Answer calls and react to key presses, the shape of an IVR or auto-attendant:

use rvoip_sip::{CallHandlerDecision, CallbackPeer, Config, Result};

# async fn example() -> Result<()> {
let peer = CallbackPeer::builder(Config::local("ivr", 5120))
    .on_incoming(|call| async move {
        println!("incoming call from {}", call.from);
        CallHandlerDecision::Accept
    })
    .on_dtmf(|call, digit| async move {
        if digit == '0' {
            call.transfer_blind("sip:operator@127.0.0.1:5122").await?;
        }
        Ok(())
    })
    .on_ended(|call_id, reason| async move {
        println!("call {call_id} ended: {reason:?}");
        Ok(())
    })
    .build()
    .await?;

peer.run().await
# }

Security and transports are configuration, not different APIs: SDES-SRTP in 07-secure-call-srtp, TLS in 08-tls-transport, DTLS-SRTP, G.729, AMR-NB/WB, and Opus behind Cargo features. The full surface is documented in the SIP crate README.

Path 2 — Browser and cross-transport gateways (rvoip + app)

RvoipApp declares transports, roles, and routing through one builder and runs SIP, WebRTC, and UCTP listeners on the shared Orchestrator:

rvoip = { version = "0.5.1", features = ["app"] }
use rvoip::app::*;

# async fn run() -> rvoip::app::AppResult<()> {
let app = RvoipApp::builder()
    .webrtc(
        WebRtcConfig::ws("127.0.0.1:8081")
            .allow(Role::Customer, [Capability::Text, Capability::Voice]),
    )
    .sip(
        SipConfig::bind("127.0.0.1:5060")
            .domain("callcenter.local")
            .allow(Role::Employee, [Capability::Voice])
            .registrar_users([("alice", "password123")]),
    )
    .employees(EmployeePolicy::named(["alice"]))
    .customers(CustomerPolicy::webrtc_only())
    .assignment(AssignmentPolicy::fixed("alice"))
    .on_message(|ctx, msg| async move {
        ctx.reply("Alice", format!("Alice received: {}", msg.text)).await
    })
    .build()
    .await?;

app.run().await
# }

Start from 12-customer-escalation-sip-webrtc: a browser chat escalates to a SIP agent's phone. For SIP into Amazon Connect, see 13-sip-to-amazon-connect.

Path 3 — Voice AI (rvoip + vapi or voip-3)

  • Hosted agent. rvoip-vapi speaks Vapi's bidirectional raw-audio WebSocket directly. Your SIP or WebRTC caller is bridged to the agent through the Orchestrator; the agent joins as its own AI participant with typed events, control messages, and supervised teardown. Start from 14-vapi-agent, one server that accepts either kind of caller. Attaching an agent to a caller you already hold:

    use std::sync::Arc;
use rvoip::Orchestrator;
use rvoip::core_traits::ids::ConnectionId;
use rvoip::vapi::{VapiAdapter, VapiApiKey, VapiAssistant, VapiCallOptions, VapiConfig};

# async fn attach(orchestrator: Arc<Orchestrator>, caller: ConnectionId)
# -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let key = VapiApiKey::new(std::env::var("VAPI_API_KEY")?)?;
let adapter = VapiAdapter::new(VapiConfig::new(key))?;
let options = VapiCallOptions::new(VapiAssistant::saved(std::env::var("VAPI_ASSISTANT_ID")?));

// Joins a distinct AI participant, originates the agent leg, bridges audio.
let mut call = adapter.attach_agent(&orchestrator, caller, options).await?;
call.say("One moment while I look that up.", false, true).await?;
let _outcome = call.wait().await;
# Ok(())
# }

  • Your own pipeline. rvoip-harness gives you ASR, TTS, dialog, and recording provider traits, and rvoip-vcon emits signed vCon records of the conversation. 11-ai-harness-demo runs the whole loop with deterministic providers, so you can see the shape before you plug in a real model.

How it fits together

Every transport turns into the same objects, so an application written against the conversation model does not care whether a leg arrived over SIP, a browser, or QUIC. That is what lets one Orchestrator bridge them.

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Your application                                                  │
│ softphone · PBX · contact center · browser gateway · AI agent     │
└───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                                │  rvoip-sip  /  rvoip (+ features)
┌───────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐
│ Shared conversation model  (rvoip-core)                           │
│ Orchestrator · Conversation · Session · Participant · Connection  │
│ routing · admission · bridges · media graph · events              │
└──────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────┘
               │                │                │
        ┌──────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼───────────────┐
        │ SIP + RTP   │  │ WebRTC      │  │ UCTP                 │
        │ UDP/TCP/TLS │  │ ICE/DTLS    │  │ QUIC/WebTransport/WS │
        └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬───────────────┘
               └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                                │
             ┌──────────────────▼───────────────────┐
             │ Optional products and extensions      │
             │ Vapi · AI harness · vCon · MoQ        │
             │ Amazon Connect · identity · audit     │
             └───────────────────────────────────────┘

Words you will meet in the API:

  • Conversation — the thing people are in together. It outlives any one connection.
  • Session — one participant's time in a conversation.
  • Participant — a human or an AI agent. Roles (Agent, Observer, customer) can change without moving connections.
  • Connection — one transport leg: a SIP dialog, a browser peer connection, a UCTP session.
  • Stream — the audio (or video, or data) flowing on a connection. Bridges join streams across connections, transcoding when codecs differ.

Adapters depend on the shared ConnectionAdapter trait; the core never imports a transport. The design docs go deeper, starting with INTERFACE_DESIGN.md and CONVERSATION_PROTOCOL.md.

What ships today

The WebRTC implementation of ICE and DTLS-SRTP is separate from the SIP beta claim. UCTP and MoQ availability does not imply that SIP-over-QUIC or RTP-over-QUIC has shipped.

Extensions

All 14 extension crates ship at 0.5.1. They stay optional so protocol crates depend on provider contracts, never on a deployment backend.

Group Extensions Available capability
AI and conversation data rvoip-harness, rvoip-vapi, rvoip-vcon, rvoip-vcon-postgres ASR/TTS/dialog/recording provider traits, native Vapi agents, signed vCon artifacts, Postgres storage

How they attach: voip-3 on the facade brings in the harness, vCon, and the identity surface; vapi and sip-stir-shaken are their own facade features; everything else is a direct dependency.

rvoip = { version = "0.5.1", features = ["sip", "vapi", "sip-stir-shaken"] }
rvoip-keycloak = "0.5.1"
rvoip-redis = "0.5.1"
rvoip-audit = "0.5.1"

The contracts they implement live in rvoip-auth-core, rvoip-users-core, and rvoip-identity.

Workspace map

For orientation only. Everything below the front doors is a transitive dependency of rvoip or rvoip-sip; depend on it directly only when you are extending the platform itself.

Family Crates
Front doors rvoip, rvoip-sip, rvoip-client
Foundation rvoip-core, rvoip-core-traits, rvoip-infra-common
SIP internals rvoip-sip-core, rvoip-sip-transport, rvoip-sip-dialog, rvoip-sip-proxy, rvoip-sip-registrar
Media rvoip-media-core, rvoip-codec-core, rvoip-rtp-core, rvoip-ice-core, rvoip-audio-send-queue, rvoip-audio-device
WebRTC and Connect rvoip-webrtc, rvoip-rtc, rvoip-webrtc-stack, rvoip-amazon-connect
UCTP rvoip-uctp, rvoip-quic, rvoip-webtransport, rvoip-websocket
MoQ rvoip-moq, rvoip-moq-transport, rvoip-moq-native, rvoip-moq-relay
Identity rvoip-auth-core, rvoip-users-core, rvoip-identity
Extensions The 14 extension crates above

SIP interoperability and release evidence

The full release path exercises rvoip-sip public APIs against independently implemented peers. The exact peer versions, scenarios, transports, results, and exclusions are recorded in signed qualification evidence; see the compatibility matrix.

Patch releases can explicitly use the shorter release path: unit, integration, regression, example, and doc tests, including runnable TURN/ICE examples, without benchmark, soak/load, or extended interoperability jobs. Each GitHub release links its tested commit and gate results; a reduced patch report marks performance qualification NOT RUN. The matrix below describes the full qualification scope, not a claim that a patch run repeated it.

Peer/tool Status Executed scope
Asterisk Release-gated Endpoint, StreamPeer, and CallbackPeer; registration, calls/media, codecs, hold/resume, ring-cancel, RFC 4733 DTMF, rejection, and blind transfer over the documented UDP and TLS profiles
FreeSWITCH Release-gated The corresponding public-API, scenario, codec, and transport matrix
Jambonz OSS 0.9.15 Release-gated Revision- and digest-pinned Jambonz SBC/registrar/RTPengine profile across the applicable public-API UDP/plain-RTP matrix
SIPp Release-gated Standards scenarios and bounded signaling-load profiles
baresip Release-gated External strict user-agent call against the RVoIP SIP listener
Kamailio Release-gated RFC 3261 transaction-stateful proxy in both hop orders over UDP, TCP, and TLS, plus registrar-proxy with an rtpengine media relay: registration, calls, AMR in all four framings, DTMF, SDES-SRTP
OpenSIPS Release-gated The same proxy matrix in both hop orders over UDP, TCP, and TLS, and the same rtpengine lab scope

SIP interoperability attestation

The strict full-beta gate requires an explicit PASS attestation for every required independently managed peer below. The report generator binds each row to the tested source tree, exact peer identity and configuration, selected matrix, and hashed evidence; it refuses to produce a strict release-candidate report if a required peer is missing, skipped, ambiguous, unpinned, or failing.

Peer Attested boundary Required release evidence
Asterisk PBX/B2BUA call control and RTP media Provider-specific all-PASS rows from the recorded API, scenario, codec, and security matrix, plus the exact local revision and configuration fingerprint
FreeSWITCH PBX/B2BUA call control and RTP media Provider-specific all-PASS rows from the recorded API, scenario, codec, and security matrix, plus the exact local revision and configuration fingerprint
Jambonz OSS SBC/B2BUA, registrar, and anchored RTP media Latest-version check, source and image pins, all-PASS applicable public-API UDP/plain-RTP matrix, and post-run cleanup
Kamailio RFC 3261 transaction-stateful proxy interoperability Digest-pinned peer, both hop orders, UDP/TCP/TLS, packet assertions, verified TLS evidence, and post-retention cleanup
OpenSIPS RFC 3261 transaction-stateful proxy interoperability Digest-pinned peer, both hop orders, UDP/TCP/TLS, packet assertions, verified TLS evidence, and post-retention cleanup

The 0.5.1 release uses the shorter patch profile: regular unit, integration, regression, example, and doc tests, including TURN/ICE checks. Benchmarks and extended external interoperability were not rerun. See the 0.5.1 release notes and the release's qualification attachments for exact commands, results, and scope.

Historical full-release evidence, retained at its original versions:

  • Qualification report — exact versions, row counts, scenarios, hashes, PASS status.
  • Performance report.
  • RFC 7501/7502 benchmark report: sustained Session Establishment Rates for published 0.5.0 on one c8i.4xlarge, reported in IETF format (R1 TLS 8,348 and R5 UDP 8,256 sessions/s without media; R2 TLS+SRTP 1,124 and R6 UDP+RTP 1,204 with media).
  • RFC evidence matrix and security posture.
  • Interop plan — the evidence boundaries.
  • Changelog, release notes and the 0.4 migration guide — what changed in this release and how to upgrade from 0.3.

This is bounded interoperability evidence, not a claim of compatibility with every version, module, configuration, transport, codec, or SIP extension, and not carrier certification. Anything outside a stated qualification boundary remains the application's responsibility to validate in its own deployment.

Developer-preview products document their own supported scope and gaps in their crate READMEs. A published crate or Cargo feature is evidence of availability, not a blanket production-readiness statement.

Building and testing the workspace

git clone https://github.com/eisenzopf/rvoip.git
cd rvoip

# Build the default workspace members
cargo build

# Run a working SIP call
cargo run -p rvoip-sip --example endpoint_local_call

# Run the workspace test suite
scripts/test_all.sh

Feature-gated targets (codecs, DTLS-SRTP, generated compliance suites) only build with their features on; use --all-features when you touch a gated path. docs/RELEASING.md describes the release train.

Roadmap

Remaining major items, beyond the developer-preview products above:

  • SIP-over-QUIC and RTP-over-QUIC (RoQ) transport profiles.
  • Integrated multi-party SFU/MCU products beyond the existing media primitives.
  • Production graduation of AAuth as its standards work and deployment evidence mature.
  • Deeper AI participants with multi-agent orchestration beyond today's provider harness.
  • Additional qualification and release gates for the developer-preview products.

Detailed engineering gaps are tracked in docs/GAP_PLAN.md and in issues.

Contributing

  • Bugs: open an issue with reproduction steps.
  • Feature requests: use discussions or issues and describe the target product and compatibility expectations.
  • Pull requests: workspace-wide tests run through scripts/test_all.sh.
